title: Jerusalem Defended, Then a Nation Mourns
overview: The LORD promises to make Jerusalem impossible for attacking nations to defeat, then describes its people moved to deep, family-by-family mourning over someone they have pierced.

parts.label: The Maker of everything speaks (v. 1)
parts.note: The word translated "prophecy" can also mean a burden, a heavy message that weighs on those it concerns. The speaker is introduced as the one who made the sky, the earth and the human spirit, a reminder that he has the power to do what follows.

parts.label: A cup and a heavy stone (vv. 2-3)
parts.note: Nations that attack Jerusalem will be like people gulping a drink that leaves them staggering, or like someone straining to lift a stone too heavy for them and hurting themselves. An old tradition links the stone to a local test of strength by lifting heavy rocks, but either way the point is that attacking the city will backfire.

parts.label: Panic among the attackers (vv. 4-5)
parts.note: Horses and riders, the most feared weapon of the day, are struck with panic, madness and blindness, while the LORD keeps his eyes open over Judah. Seeing this, the leaders of the surrounding countryside recognize that Jerusalem's strength really comes from its God.

parts.label: Judah and David's family made strong (vv. 6-9)
parts.note: In violent battle imagery, Judah's leaders become like fire dropped into dry wood, burning up the nations around them, and the countryside is rescued first so the royal family and the capital are not honored above the rest of Judah. The weakest person in Jerusalem will be as strong as King David, and David's family will be like the angel of the LORD who once led Israel through the desert.

parts.label: Grief for the pierced one (v. 10)
parts.note: The scene turns from outer rescue to inner change, as God gives a spirit that moves people to plead for mercy, and they look on the one they pierced and grieve as parents grieve an only child. The text shifts between "me" and "him", so who was pierced is unclear and much debated; Christians read it as Jesus, since John's Gospel quotes this verse at his crucifixion.

parts.label: Every family mourns apart (vv. 11-14)
parts.note: The mourning at Hadad Rimmon near Megiddo probably recalls the national grief for good King Josiah, killed in battle there, though some scholars think it refers to a local mourning ritual. Families, and husbands and wives, mourn separately, from royal clans (David, Nathan) to priestly ones (Levi, Shimei), so the grief is both nationwide and deeply personal.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this chapter mainly describes a future, end-times rescue of Jerusalem in which the Jewish people come to recognize Jesus, or whether it is fulfilled more broadly and spiritually through the crucifixion and the church.
think: What do you think it would take for a whole community to grieve honestly over a harm it had a part in causing?
